title: Next in line
q: Presidents who first took office when their predecessor died or resigned
rule: Counts even if they later won election in their own right; vice presidents elected directly, like Nixon and Biden, do not.
fact: Gerald Ford is the only person to have served as both vice president and president without ever being elected to either office.

traps.Richard Nixon: He was Eisenhower's vice president but won the 1968 election outright.
traps.Joe Biden: He was Obama's vice president but won the 2020 election outright.
traps.George H. W. Bush: Neither Bush moved up mid-term: the father won in 1988, the son in 2000.
traps.Martin Van Buren: He moved up from vice president by winning the 1836 election.
traps.John Adams: He became president by winning the 1796 election, not by succession.

title: Short and sweet
q: Presidents whose surname has just one syllable
rule: Judged by how the surname is spoken; both Presidents Bush count, and Trump counts once.
fact: Rutherford B. Hayes won the 1876 election by a single electoral vote, 185 to 184, despite losing the popular vote.

title: Bad ends
q: Of the Twelve Caesars, those who were killed or took their own lives
rule: The dictator who heads the list counts; the rumoured poisonings and smotherings of Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius do not.
fact: Galba, Otho and Vitellius all met violent ends within the single year AD 69, and Otho's reign lasted only about three months.

traps.Augustus: He died in his bed at Nola in AD 14; the poisoning story is only a rumour.
traps.Claudius: Probably poisoned, but the ancient sources disagree and it is not settled.
traps.Tiberius: He died at Misenum in AD 37, and the smothering tale is unproven.
traps.Vespasian: He died of illness in AD 79, reportedly joking about becoming a god.
traps.Titus: He died of a fever in AD 81, aged just 41.

title: Last post
q: UK Prime Ministers who died while still in office
rule: Counts from Walpole's era onwards; anyone who resigned first, however shortly before dying, does not count.
fact: George Canning died in office in 1827 after only 119 days, the shortest premiership on record until Liz Truss's 49 days in 2022.

traps.Winston Churchill: He left office in 1955 and died in 1965.
traps.Neville Chamberlain: He resigned in May 1940 and died that November.
traps.Henry Campbell-Bannerman: He resigned in April 1908, a few weeks before he died.
traps.Bonar Law: He resigned in May 1923 and died that October.
traps.Robert Peel: He died after a riding accident in 1850, four years after leaving office.

title: Double-barrelled
q: UK Prime Ministers with a hyphenated surname
rule: The surname as normally written must have a hyphen (so not Churchill or Lloyd George); peers may be given by title.
fact: Henry Campbell-Bannerman added 'Bannerman' to his surname in 1871, when he inherited a wealthy uncle's estate.

traps.David Lloyd George: His double-barrelled name was written without a hyphen.
traps.Lloyd George: His double-barrelled name was written without a hyphen.
traps.Winston Churchill: Born Spencer-Churchill, but he normally used plain Churchill.
traps.Boris Johnson: No hyphen: 'de Pfeffel' is one of his middle names.
traps.Theresa May: No hyphen; she was born Theresa Brasier.

title: Greek in disguise
q: Greek capital letters that look just like a Latin capital letter
rule: Judged in a standard font. Letters like delta, gamma, sigma, pi and omega match no Latin capital.
fact: 'Xmas' is not a secular dodge: the X is the Greek capital Chi, the first letter of Christos, which happens to look like a Latin X.

traps.Omega: Ω is a horseshoe shape, not any Latin capital.
traps.Delta: Δ is a triangle, which no Latin capital resembles.
traps.Pi: Π is a table shape, not any Latin capital.
traps.Sigma: Σ is not shaped like any Latin capital.
traps.Gamma: Γ is not shaped like any Latin capital.

title: Four-letter words
q: Books of the Bible with four letters or fewer in their name
rule: Uses the 66-book Protestant Bible. Ignore numbering, so a numbered book counts under its name.
fact: Job has the shortest name of any Bible book at three letters, yet it runs to 42 chapters.

title: Class of '49
q: The twelve founding members of NATO
rule: Countries that signed the North Atlantic Treaty in April 1949; later joiners such as West Germany and Spain do not count.
fact: Iceland, a NATO founder, has never had a standing army, and Portugal joined in 1949 while still under Salazar's dictatorship.

traps.Spain: Franco's Spain stayed out; it joined in 1982.
traps.Greece: Greece and Turkey joined together in 1952.
traps.Sweden: Sweden stayed neutral until it joined in 2024.

title: Eastern bloc
q: The eight original signatories of the Warsaw Pact
rule: The states that signed in 1955, with the country that later split in two counting once. Cuba, Mongolia and Yugoslavia were never members.
fact: Albania stopped taking part in 1961 and formally quit in 1968, weeks after the pact's armies invaded Czechoslovakia.

traps.Yugoslavia: Tito broke with Stalin in 1948 and stayed non-aligned.
traps.Cuba: A Soviet ally, but never a member of the pact.
traps.Mongolia: A Soviet ally, but never a full member of the pact.
traps.China: Communist, but never a member of the pact.
traps.Ukraine: It was a Soviet republic, not a separate signatory.

title: Remember, remember
q: The thirteen conspirators in the 1605 Gunpowder Plot
rule: The thirteen plotters traditionally named; priests and informers such as Henry Garnet do not count.
fact: The plot's leader was Robert Catesby, not Fawkes; he was shot dead at Holbeche House three days after Fawkes was arrested.

traps.Henry Garnet: A Jesuit priest executed for knowing of the plot, but not one of the thirteen.
traps.Lord Monteagle: He received the anonymous warning letter that exposed the plot.
traps.Robert Cecil: He was the king's spymaster who helped to uncover the plot.
traps.King James: He was the target of the plot, not a plotter.

title: Hill walk
q: The seven hills of Rome in the traditional list
rule: Only the traditional seven count; the Pincian, Vatican and Janiculum hills are not among them.
fact: The English word 'palace' comes from the Palatine, the hill where Rome's emperors built their residences.

traps.Vatican: Vatican Hill is across the Tiber, outside the traditional seven.
traps.Janiculum: It rises on the Tiber's west bank, so it is not one of the seven.
traps.Pincian: The Pincio was outside the old city and is not one of the seven.
traps.Monte Testaccio: It is a mound of discarded Roman amphorae, not a natural hill.
traps.Colosseum: It stands in a valley between hills and is not a hill itself.

title: Title role
q: English kings who give their name to a Shakespeare history play
rule: Histories printed in the First Folio only; Scottish or legendary kings and the disputed Edward III do not count.
fact: A cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight and burned down the Globe in June 1613.

traps.Macbeth: He was a King of Scotland, not of England.
traps.King Lear: A legendary king of ancient Britain, not a historical English monarch.
traps.Henry VII: Shakespeare wrote no play named for the first Tudor king.
traps.Edward II: That play is by Christopher Marlowe, not Shakespeare.
traps.Edward III: Only partly attributed to Shakespeare, and not in the First Folio.

King John: The Life and Death of King John

title: Stuart times
q: Monarchs who ruled England between Elizabeth I and George I
rule: Joint monarchs count separately; Lord Protectors do not count as monarchs.
fact: Mary II ruled jointly with her husband William III from 1689 until she died of smallpox in 1694 aged 32, after which William reigned alone until 1702.

traps.Oliver Cromwell: He ruled as Lord Protector and refused the crown when it was offered.
traps.Richard Cromwell: Oliver's son was Lord Protector for under a year, never king.
traps.Bonnie Prince Charlie: He was a Jacobite claimant who never reigned.
traps.Mary, Queen of Scots: She was executed in 1587, during Elizabeth I's reign.
traps.Lady Jane Grey: Her nine-day reign in 1553 came long before Elizabeth I.

title: Tudor brides
q: Women who were queen consort to a Tudor king
rule: Wives of Henry VII and Henry VIII only; Mary I's husband was a king consort and Elizabeth I never married.
fact: Elizabeth of York was the daughter of Edward IV, the niece of Richard III, the wife of Henry VII and the mother of Henry VIII.

traps.Mary Boleyn: Anne's sister was Henry VIII's mistress, never his queen.
traps.Lady Jane Grey: She was a queen regnant for nine days, not a consort.
traps.Elizabeth Woodville: She was queen to Edward IV, before the Tudors.
traps.Anne Neville: She was queen to Richard III, the last Plantagenet king.
traps.Margaret Beaufort: She was Henry VII's mother and was never queen.

title: Before England
q: The seven kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy
rule: The traditional list of seven; smaller sub-kingdoms and Celtic kingdoms do not count.
fact: Wessex alone survived the Viking invasions, and Alfred the Great's grandson Athelstan became the first king of all England in 927.

traps.Cornwall: It was part of the British kingdom of Dumnonia, not an Anglo-Saxon kingdom.
traps.Danelaw: A Viking-ruled region of the 9th century on, not one of the seven.
traps.Bernicia: It merged with Deira to form Northumbria rather than standing alone.
traps.Lindsey: A small sub-kingdom in Lincolnshire, absorbed by its larger neighbours.
traps.Northumberland: The modern county covers only the far north of old Northumbria.

title: Next door up
q: Prime Ministers who had earlier been Chancellor of the Exchequer
rule: Only PMs who took office in 1900 or later, and who held the Chancellorship before becoming PM.
fact: John Major was Foreign Secretary for only three months in 1989 and Chancellor for 13 months before becoming PM in November 1990.

traps.George Osborne: Six years as Chancellor, but he never became PM.
traps.Rab Butler: Chancellor in the 1950s, passed over for PM in 1957 and 1963.
traps.Denis Healey: Labour's Chancellor from 1974 to 1979, never PM.
traps.Margaret Thatcher: She was Education Secretary and never Chancellor.
traps.Tony Blair: He held no ministerial post at all before becoming PM.

title: Passport control
q: UK Prime Ministers born outside England
rule: Any birthplace outside England counts, at home or abroad.
fact: Bonar Law, born in New Brunswick, was the first PM born outside the British Isles; Boris Johnson, born in New York City, was the second.

traps.Winston Churchill: Born at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, though his mother was American.
traps.David Lloyd George: Raised in Wales and Welsh-speaking, but born in Manchester.
traps.Alec Douglas-Home: A Scottish aristocrat, but born in London.
traps.Lord Rosebery: A Scottish earl, but born in Mayfair, London.
traps.William Gladstone: His family was Scottish, but he was born in Liverpool.

title: Original thirteen
q: The thirteen British colonies that became the first US states
rule: The two Carolinas count separately.
fact: Delaware ratified the Constitution first, on 7 December 1787, and now calls itself the First State.

traps.Maine: It was part of Massachusetts until 1820.
traps.Vermont: It was disputed between New York and New Hampshire and joined in 1791.
traps.Kentucky: It was part of Virginia until 1792.
traps.Florida: Britain held it only from 1763 to 1783, and it stayed loyal in 1776.
traps.West Virginia: It split from Virginia in 1863 during the Civil War.

title: Divided house
q: States that seceded from the Union in 1860 and 1861
rule: The eleven that formally seceded; Kentucky and Missouri, which had rival Confederate governments, did not.
fact: Tennessee was the last state to secede, in June 1861, and the first to be readmitted to the Union, in July 1866.

traps.Kentucky: It declared neutrality, then stayed in the Union.
traps.Missouri: A rival Confederate government existed, but the state never seceded.
traps.Maryland: A slave state that stayed in the Union.
traps.Delaware: A slave state that stayed loyal to the Union.
traps.West Virginia: It broke away from Virginia in 1863 to stay in the Union.

title: Capital idea
q: Cities where Congress met before it settled in Washington, D.C.
rule: Includes meetings of the Continental Congress and the Confederation Congress; a one-day stay still counts.
fact: Lancaster, Pennsylvania was the capital of the United States for a single day, 27 September 1777, as Congress fled the British advance on Philadelphia.

traps.Boston: Congress never sat there, despite the city's role in the Revolution.
traps.Williamsburg: It was the capital of colonial Virginia, not of the United States.
traps.Richmond: It was the capital of the Confederacy, not of the United States.
traps.Washington: It is the permanent capital that Congress moved to in 1800.

title: Herculean tasks
q: The twelve labours of Hercules
rule: Name the creature or prize at the heart of each labour.
fact: For his eighth labour Heracles fed King Diomedes to his own man-eating mares, which in the usual telling then became tame enough to lead away.

traps.Minotaur: Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Cretan labyrinth.
traps.Chimera: That was Bellerophon's feat, riding Pegasus.
traps.Golden Fleece: That was Jason's quest with the Argonauts.
traps.Sphinx: Oedipus defeated the Sphinx by solving its riddle.

title: Muse on this
q: The nine Muses of Greek mythology
fact: The word museum comes from the Greek mouseion, a shrine of the Muses, who were daughters of Zeus and the Titaness Mnemosyne, goddess of memory.

traps.Apollo: The god who led the Muses, but not himself a Muse.
traps.Mnemosyne: The Titaness of memory, and the Muses' mother.
traps.Sappho: Plato called her the tenth Muse, but she was a mortal poet.
traps.Athena: A goddess of wisdom and crafts, not one of the nine.

title: Before Zeus
q: The twelve original Titans, children of Gaia and Uranus
rule: Second-generation Titans such as Atlas and Prometheus do not count.
fact: Cronus swallowed five of his children; his wife and sister Rhea saved the sixth, Zeus, by handing him a stone wrapped in baby clothes.

traps.Atlas: A son of the Titan Iapetus, so second generation.
traps.Prometheus: A son of Iapetus, so second generation.
traps.Helios: A child of Hyperion and Theia, so second generation.
traps.Zeus: Cronus's son and king of the Olympians, who overthrew the Titans.
traps.Epimetheus: A son of Iapetus and brother of Prometheus.

title: When in Rome
q: Roman names for Olympian gods that differ from their Greek names
rule: Give the Roman name; Apollo kept the same name in both cultures, so he does not count.
fact: Ceres gave us the word cereal, Vulcan gave us volcano and Bacchus gave us bacchanal.

traps.Zeus: That is the Greek name; the Roman form is Jupiter.
traps.Athena: That is the Greek name; the Roman form is Minerva.
traps.Apollo: Greeks and Romans used exactly the same name for him.
traps.Pluto: He is Hades's Roman name, but Hades is not counted among the twelve Olympians.
traps.Cupid: He is the Roman Eros, who was never one of the twelve Olympians.

title: Rome's kings
q: The seven traditional kings of Rome, before the Republic
rule: The traditional list of seven; historians doubt how much of it is real.
fact: Tradition credits Ancus Marcius with founding Ostia, Rome's port at the mouth of the Tiber, and building the first bridge over the river.

traps.Remus: Romulus's twin brother, killed before Rome had a king.
traps.Lucius Junius Brutus: He helped expel the last king and became one of the first consuls.
traps.Julius Caesar: He was dictator for life and refused a crown.
traps.Augustus: He was the first emperor, centuries after the kings.
traps.Cincinnatus: He was a dictator of the early Republic, not a king.

title: Golden age
q: Roman emperors who reigned between AD 96 and AD 192
rule: Co-emperors count too.
fact: Commodus was strangled in his bath by his wrestling partner Narcissus in AD 192, not killed in the arena as the film Gladiator shows.

traps.Domitian: He was assassinated in AD 96, just before Nerva took over.
traps.Pertinax: He briefly took the throne in AD 193 after Commodus.
traps.Septimius Severus: He seized power in AD 193, the year after Commodus died.
traps.Nero: He died in AD 68, nearly three decades earlier.
traps.Constantine: He reigned in the 4th century, long after Commodus.

title: The Great Nine
q: The nine gods of the Great Ennead of Heliopolis
rule: The classic nine of Heliopolis. Later additions such as Horus do not count.
fact: Shu, the god of air, is shown holding up his daughter Nut, the sky, to keep her apart from her brother and husband Geb, the earth.

traps.Anubis: The jackal-headed god of embalming is not one of the nine.
traps.Thoth: The ibis-headed god of writing is not one of the nine.
traps.Bastet: The cat goddess is not one of the nine.
traps.Hathor: The cow goddess of love and music is not one of the nine.

title: Name that day
q: The gods and heavenly bodies that the English weekdays are named after
rule: Sunday to Saturday. Friday's goddess is disputed between two names, and both are accepted.
fact: English swapped the Roman gods Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus for the Norse Tyr, Odin, Thor and Frigg, but left Saturn with his Roman name.

traps.Mars: He names mardi in French, not Tuesday.
traps.Mercury: He names mercredi in French, not Wednesday.
traps.Jupiter: He names jeudi in French, not Thursday.
traps.Venus: She names vendredi in French, not Friday.
traps.Loki: The Norse trickster never had a weekday named after him.

title: Divine descents
q: The traditional avatars of Vishnu in the Dashavatara
rule: Traditions differ over one of the ten, so both versions are accepted.
fact: Narasimha, half man and half lion, killed the demon Hiranyakashipu at dusk, on a threshold, on his lap, sidestepping every term of the demon's boon.

traps.Hanuman: Rama's devoted follower, not an avatar of Vishnu.
traps.Ganesha: The elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati.
traps.Shiva: A separate supreme deity, not an avatar of Vishnu.
traps.Arjuna: Krishna's friend and pupil in the Mahabharata, not an avatar.
traps.Garuda: The eagle who serves as Vishnu's mount.

title: The Twelve
q: The twelve original apostles of Jesus
rule: The betrayer counts; later apostles such as Matthias, Paul and Barnabas do not.
fact: Thaddaeus, also known as Jude, is revered by many Catholics as the patron saint of lost causes.

traps.Paul: He called himself an apostle but was never one of the Twelve.
traps.Matthias: He was chosen by lot to replace Judas after the original Twelve.
traps.Mary Magdalene: A follower of Jesus, but not one of the Twelve.
traps.Mark: A Gospel writer, but not one of the Twelve.
traps.Luke: A Gospel writer and companion of Paul, not one of the Twelve.

title: Pharaoh's problems
q: The ten plagues of Egypt in the Book of Exodus
rule: Name each plague by its subject; the usual alternative translations are accepted.
fact: At the Passover seder, Jewish families spill a drop of wine from their cups for each of the ten plagues, to show sorrow at the Egyptians' suffering.

traps.Rats: Not one of the ten plagues in Exodus.
traps.Drought: Not listed; the Nile turned to blood instead.
traps.Famine: Not one of the ten named in Exodus.
traps.Snakes: Moses's staff became a serpent as a sign, not a plague.
traps.Earthquake: Not one of the ten plagues.

title: Minor league
q: The twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament
rule: The twelve short books at the end of the Old Testament. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel are major prophets.
fact: The minor prophets are minor only in length: Obadiah, at 21 verses, is the shortest book in the Old Testament.

traps.Isaiah: A major prophet, with the longest of the prophetic books.
traps.Jeremiah: A major prophet, author of the book that bears his name.
traps.Ezekiel: A major prophet, known for his vision of the dry bones.
traps.Daniel: Counted among the major prophets in Christian Bibles.
traps.Elijah: A great prophet, but he has no book of his own.

title: Calendar revolution
q: The twelve months of the French Revolutionary calendar
rule: Accents are optional; the extra festival days at the end of the year do not count.
fact: The calendar began on 22 September 1792 with ten-day weeks and months named for weather and harvests, and Napoleon scrapped it on 1 January 1806.

traps.Janvier: That is the ordinary Gregorian January, not a Revolutionary month.
traps.Avril: That is the ordinary Gregorian April, not a Revolutionary month.
traps.Décadi: That was the tenth day of the Revolutionary week, not a month.
traps.Sansculottides: Those were the five or six festival days added at the end of the year.

title: Seeing double
q: US Presidents with a double letter in their surname
rule: The double letter must be in the surname; first names such as Jimmy and Woodrow do not count.
fact: Calvin Coolidge, born on 4 July 1872, is the only US president born on Independence Day.

traps.Jimmy Carter: The double m is in his first name, not his surname.
traps.Bill Clinton: The double l is in his first name, not his surname.
traps.Woodrow Wilson: The double o is in his first name, not his surname.
traps.William McKinley: The double l is in his first name, not his surname.
traps.Richard Nixon: Neither Richard nor Nixon has a double letter.

title: Vowel play
q: Books of the Bible whose names begin with a vowel
rule: The 66 books of the Protestant Bible; Catholic extras such as Ecclesiasticus do not count.
fact: Esther, one of only two books named for a woman, never mentions God by name in its Hebrew text.

traps.Ecclesiasticus: A Catholic deuterocanonical book, not among the 66.
traps.Esdras: An Apocrypha book, not among the 66.
traps.Hebrews: It begins with H, which is not a vowel.
traps.Judges: It begins with J, which is not a vowel.

title: Kremlin chiefs
q: The men who led the Soviet Union between 1922 and 1991
rule: The eight people usually listed as leader of the USSR, from its founder to its last. Yeltsin and Putin led Russia, not the Soviet Union.
fact: Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko all died in office within 28 months, from November 1982 to March 1985, making way for Gorbachev.

traps.Leon Trotsky: Lenin's rival lost the power struggle to Stalin and was exiled.
traps.Boris Yeltsin: He led Russia after the USSR dissolved in December 1991.
traps.Vyacheslav Molotov: Long-serving foreign minister, but never the top leader.
traps.Lavrentiy Beria: The secret police chief lost the power struggle in 1953.
traps.Alexei Kosygin: Premier under Brezhnev, who held the real power.

title: Big Bang
q: The ten countries that joined the EU on 1 May 2004
fact: Eight of the ten were former communist states, and with about 75 million new citizens it was the biggest single enlargement in EU history.

traps.Romania: It joined in 2007, in the next wave.
traps.Bulgaria: It joined in 2007, in the next wave.
traps.Croatia: It joined in 2013 and is the newest wave before today.
traps.Turkey: A long-standing candidate that has never joined.
traps.Austria: It joined in 1995, with Sweden and Finland.

title: Opposite numbers
q: The seven virtues set against the seven deadly sins
rule: Only the seven heavenly virtues, one opposing each sin; faith, hope, prudence and fortitude are excluded.
fact: The idea of virtues fighting vices goes back to Prudentius's Psychomachia, a battle poem written around AD 400.

traps.Pride: A deadly sin, not a virtue; humility is the virtue set against it.
traps.Faith: A theological virtue, not one of the seven heavenly virtues.
traps.Hope: A theological virtue, not one of the seven heavenly virtues.
traps.Prudence: A cardinal virtue, so it isn't in this set.

title: Last stand
q: Norse gods who die in Ragnarök or live through it
rule: Baldr and Höðr, who come back afterwards, don't count; giants, monsters and goddesses don't either.
fact: Módi and Magni, sons of Thor, are said to inherit his hammer Mjölnir after Ragnarök.

traps.Baldr: He dies before Ragnarök and returns afterwards, so he doesn't count.
traps.Surtr: A fire giant who kills Freyr, but he is a giant, not a god.
traps.Fenrir: The wolf that swallows Odin, but he is a monster, not a god.
traps.Jörmungandr: The serpent Thor kills, but it is a serpent, not a god.
traps.Frigg: Odin's wife, but she has no named fate at Ragnarök.

title: Pole position
q: Men who stood at the South Pole during the 1911–12 race
rule: Only men who reached the Pole itself with the Norwegian or British parties; support teams and turn-backs don't count.
fact: Amundsen reached the Pole on 14 December 1911; Scott's party arrived on 17 January 1912 and found the Norwegian tent and a letter.

traps.Ernest Shackleton: He turned back about 100 miles short of the Pole in 1909.
traps.Edmund Hillary: He reached the Pole in 1958, decades after this race.
traps.Richard Byrd: He flew over the Pole in 1929, not in this race.
traps.Robert Peary: He claimed the North Pole in 1909, not the South.

title: Wonder years
q: The seven wonders on the classic Greek list of the ancient world
rule: Only the traditional list of seven; later monuments such as the Colosseum don't count.
fact: The Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze of the sun god Helios, was felled by an earthquake around 226 BC and probably never straddled the harbour.

traps.Stonehenge: A prehistoric monument, and never on the classic list.
traps.Colosseum: A Roman arena, and never on the classic list.
traps.Great Wall of China: Often called a wonder, but never on the classic list.
traps.Taj Mahal: Built in the 1600s, long after the classic list was drawn up.

title: Trivial matters
q: The seven liberal arts taught in medieval universities
rule: Only the trivium and quadrivium; philosophy, theology and law don't count.
fact: Trivium means 'three ways' in Latin and quadrivium means 'four ways'; together they make up the seven liberal arts.

traps.Philosophy: Central to medieval universities, but not one of the seven arts.
traps.Theology: The highest faculty, but not one of the seven arts.
traps.Law: A medieval faculty, but not one of the seven arts.
traps.Medicine: A higher faculty, but not one of the seven arts.
